title: Firewalls, NAT & VPNs: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before notes on stateless vs stateful firewalls, NAT and port forwarding, DMZ design, VPN types, IPsec vs TLS VPNs and WireGuard basics, ending with a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Firewalls: Stateless vs Stateful
points: A firewall allows or drops packets by rules matched top to bottom; the first match wins, and a default policy (usually deny) applies when nothing matches
Stateless firewall: judges each packet alone on header fields (src/dst IP, port, protocol, flags), so return traffic needs its own explicit rule
Stateful firewall: keeps a connection-tracking table (5-tuple plus state NEW, ESTABLISHED, RELATED) and auto-allows replies to allowed outbound flows
Comparison: stateless is fast and simple but weak (used in router ACLs, AWS NACLs); stateful is smarter and heavier on memory (iptables/nftables conntrack, AWS security groups, most firewalls)
Mistake: a stateless rule allowing inbound 443 but no outbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535) breaks replies, and allow rules placed after a broad deny never match

chapters.title: NAT and Port Forwarding
points: NAT rewrites IP addresses in packet headers so private RFC1918 hosts (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) can reach the internet through public IPs
Types: static NAT (1:1 mapping), dynamic NAT (pool of public IPs), PAT/NAT overload (many hosts share one public IP, told apart by source port)
SNAT/masquerade rewrites the source on outbound traffic; the NAT table remembers the mapping to translate replies back

Port forwarding is DNAT: inbound public_ip:8080 is rewritten to 192.168.1.10:80. Example: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to 192.168.1.10:80 (also needs a FORWARD allow and ip_forward=1)

Mistakes: NAT is not a security feature (the stateful filter is); forgetting net.ipv4.ip_forward=1; no hairpin NAT so inside clients cannot reach the public IP; NAT breaks end-to-end protocols such as IPsec AH

chapters.title: DMZ and Network Segmentation
points: DMZ is a separate subnet that holds public-facing servers (web, mail, reverse proxy) so a compromise does not reach the internal LAN
Three-legged firewall: one firewall with interfaces for outside, DMZ and inside. Dual-firewall design puts the DMZ between an external and an internal firewall (stronger, costs more)
Traffic rules: internet to DMZ only on needed ports; inside to DMZ allowed; DMZ to inside denied or tightly limited (for example app server to DB on one port); DMZ to internet restricted
Home-router 'DMZ host' is not a real DMZ: it forwards all ports to one device, with no segmentation
Mistakes: putting the database in the DMZ, allowing broad DMZ-to-LAN rules, and using a flat network with no isolation between DMZ servers

chapters.title: VPN Types and IPsec vs TLS
points: VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network. Site-to-site joins two networks gateway to gateway and is always on and transparent to hosts; remote access connects one user device to the network through a client
Full tunnel sends all traffic through the VPN; split tunnel sends only corporate subnets and leaves the rest direct (less load, weaker control)

IPsec works at Layer 3: IKE phase 1 sets up the secure channel and phase 2 builds the ESP tunnel. Uses UDP 500, UDP 4500 for NAT-T, and ESP (protocol 50). Tunnel mode wraps the whole packet (VPNs); transport mode protects only the payload
TLS/SSL VPN (OpenVPN, AnyConnect) works at L4-L7 over TCP/UDP 443, passes through firewalls and NAT easily, and suits remote access; IPsec suits site-to-site and needs a client or hardware support
Mistakes: mismatched IKE or phase-2 proposals or pre-shared keys, overlapping subnets at both sites, blocking ESP or UDP 500/4500, and MTU/MSS problems (lower MTU or clamp MSS)

chapters.title: WireGuard Basics
points: WireGuard is a small, fast L3 VPN in the Linux kernel that uses UDP and fixed modern crypto (Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305), with no cipher negotiation
Each peer has a keypair: wg genkey | tee private.key | wg pubkey > public.key. Peers trust each other by exchanging public keys only; never share the private key
AllowedIPs does two jobs: outgoing routing table and incoming source filter (cryptokey routing). 0.0.0.0/0 means a full tunnel
Minimal wg0.conf: [Interface] PrivateKey, Address=10.0.0.2/24, ListenPort=51820; [Peer] PublicKey, Endpoint=host:51820, AllowedIPs=10.0.0.0/24, PersistentKeepalive=25 (use it behind NAT)
Commands: wg-quick up wg0, wg-quick down wg0, wg show (check latest handshake). Mistakes: overlapping AllowedIPs between peers, no UDP port open, wrong public key, missing ip_forward on a gateway

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Firewalls, NAT and VPNs
points: Stateless = per-packet and needs return rules (NACL); stateful = conntrack table that auto-allows replies (security group, iptables)
NAT: SNAT/masquerade is outbound, DNAT is port forwarding, PAT shares one IP; NAT is not a firewall
DMZ: internet to DMZ yes, DMZ to LAN no; the database stays inside
VPN ports: IPsec = UDP 500, UDP 4500, ESP 50; TLS VPN = 443; WireGuard = UDP 51820
Debug order: check keys and proposals, then routes and AllowedIPs, then firewall ports, then MTU; use wg show, ip route and iptables -L -n -v
